problem: Pixel-based model-based generalist agents such as LEXA dream with a naive strategy (i.i.d. random sampling of start states and goals from the replay buffer). They explore inefficiently and achieve distant goals imprecisely in large, partially observable environments.
motivation: Cognitive science suggests humans plan by spatial divide-and-conquer: they first reach a familiar landmark near the destination, then navigate locally. Bringing this structure into dreaming should improve sample efficiency, exploration and goal-reaching precision of unsupervised generalist agents.
key_idea: Learn discrete latent landmarks (VQ-VAE over world-model states) and a landmark-conditioned highway policy, then use them to start exploration from curious landmarks and to move near a goal before a locally trained achiever takes over.
insight: The ablation (Fig. ablation_modules) shows both strategic exploration and strategic achievement help. The biggest gain comes from strategic achievement combined with focused sampling. Without focused sampling, performance falls back to roughly the no-strategic-achievement variant, so training the achiever on nearby start-goal pairs is what matters, and landmarks make that regime valid at test time. The Maze-15x15 analysis shows the limit: visually similar regions confuse the highway policy about which landmark it has reached.
method: Latent landmarks: a VQ-VAE with N codes (64 or 128) maps RSSM model states to discrete codes. Codes act as cluster centers and are trained with a reconstruction plus commitment loss, with code resampling against collapse.
Highway policy: a landmark-conditioned policy trained in imagination. Its reward is the negative state distance to the decoded landmark plus a K-NN particle entropy term.

Explorer and Achiever: the Explorer maximizes ensemble-disagreement reward, and imagined rollouts start from landmarks as well as replay states. The Achiever is goal-conditioned with a LEXA-style temporal-distance reward.

Curious landmark exploration: decode each landmark, imagine H-step Explorer rollouts, and score curiosity as mean exploration reward. Sample a landmark proportionally to curiosity every T_F steps, run the highway policy until T_L steps or a distance threshold, then switch to the Explorer.
Focused sampling: train the Achiever on start and goal observations taken within T_S steps in the same trajectory, so it masters local navigation.
Landmark-guided achievement: at test time encode the goal image, find the nearest landmark, run the highway policy to it, then switch to the Achiever.

setting.backbone: DreamerV2-style RSSM world model + VQ-VAE landmarks + Highway/Explorer/Achiever actor-critics (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Unsupervised online exploration data in each environment (about 2M interaction steps in 2D navigation); no external data.
setting.observation: 64x64 RGB: partially observable egocentric top-down 5x5 view (2D), first-person view (3D maze), third-person view (RoboKitchen)
setting.action_space: low-level discrete/continuous environment actions (grid-world moves in 2D, first-person maze moves in 3D, arm control in RoboKitchen)
setting.simulator: Custom 2D grid navigation, modified Memory Maze (3D), RoboKitchen (LEXA)
setting.privileged: none (goal given as an image at test time)

numbers.extra: 2M interaction steps, unseen goal images, mean over 3 seeds

numbers_note: Success rates are for custom in-house benchmarks, not standard VLN or ObjNav benchmarks. Ablation, sample-efficiency and RoboYoga results are given only in figures.
results: Dr. Strategy reaches 94.03%, 96.50% and 67.11% on 9-room, spiral 9-room and 25-room, against a best baseline (GC-Director) of 28.08%, 30.45% and 27.11%. It reaches 86.66% on Maze-7x7 versus LEXA's 51.11%, and 44.44% on Maze-15x15 versus LEXA's 41.20%. On RoboKitchen it is slightly worse than LEXA (19.44% vs 24.30%).
limitations: Weak on RoboKitchen manipulation, where the fixed third-person view gives poorly distinguishable landmarks and tasks are short-horizon.
The number of landmarks is a fixed hyperparameter, and the highway policy is confused by visually similar but distant states (Maze-15x15).
Evaluated only on self-designed, simple simulated navigation environments; the baselines are re-implemented, and the paper reports no real-robot experiments.
